  6. Documentation contribution guide (WIP)

docs.title: Why SlopeCraft?
docs.text:
Most players have already get used to pixel arts, they place blocks to form them, and look at them from far beyond or far far away. But when they learned to use map, trying to record their pixel arts by map and subsequently placing maps into item frames, something weird happens: what map represent is obviously different from what their eyes see directly.

SlopeCraft is invented to fix this difference. So pixel arts generated by SlopeCraft is not designed to be looked directly.

docs.title: Why VisualCraft?
docs.text:
You may not agree with that VisualCraft is something new, because there are lots of pixel art generators on the internet, for example, SpriteCraft. I must reckon that they are great works, and for a long time I don't think it necessary to invent it again.

By I found that there are some new techniques that are rarely tried, for example:

  1. Superimposing half-transparent blocks on non-transparent blocks to produce thousands of new colors
  2. Telling the biome where you place the pixel art so that colors of grass and leaves can be computed correctly
  3. Understanding customized block models from 3rd party resource packs.

When I learned that there are so many new skills that haven't been exploited, I decided to write a new one, VisualCraft, to bring them to reality.

docs.title: SlopeCraft Tutorial
docs.text:
This document will explain in detail how to use SlopeCraft to create 3D, flat and file-only map arts.

To eliminate ambiguity, here is the meaning of a few terms:

Term Meaning Map The item in Minecraft whose id is minecraft:filled_map Save A Minecraft game save Map art The image displayed in a map item Map data file The nbt binary file that stores map data, named like map_<i>.dat

tip

You can find the option to switch languages in the Language drop-down menu of the menu bar.

docs.title: Step 0. Image preprocessing
docs.text:
First, prepare the original image you want to turn into a map art. The image used here is the one drawn by Lancet_Corgi, thanks to Daoge for the permission.

Use Photoshop or any other software that can edit images to scale its width and height to an integer multiple of 128 pixels.

Here I scaled the image to 256×256 pixels, which happens to be the size of a 2×2 map.

(Resizing is not mandatory, and SlopeCraft does not include a feature to scale images either, but I highly recommend doing it)

Save this image.

docs.title: Step 1. Map art configuration
docs.text:
Double click SlopeCraft.exe to start it, and you will see the following window.

The three page tabs at the top represent the three steps of creating a map art:

  1. Map art configuration
  2. Import images and convert
  3. Export

Outside this software there is a fourth step: importing the files into the game.

You should now be on the map art configuration page. On this page you need to finish three small steps, each explained below.

docs.title: 1.1 Choose the game version
docs.text:
You need to set the game version the map art corresponds to.

Versions from 1.12 to 26.3 are supported at the moment. I will keep following newer versions, but will not support old versions before 1.12.

Note that 1.12~1.15 have no difference in the "image quality" of map arts: a flat map art has 51 colors and a 3D map art has 153 colors. 1.16 added 7 base colors for the nether tree, so a flat map art can use 58 colors and a 3D map art can use 174 colors. 1.17 added the colors of deepslate, raw iron block and glow lichen, so a flat map art can use 61 colors and a 3D map art can use 183 colors.

Rant: why does Mojang give the nether tree so many colors? Wouldn't more skin colors be better?

docs.title: 1.2 Choose the type of map art
docs.text:
Here you need to choose the type of map art:

  • 3D map art: achieves the richest colors and the finest image quality, at the cost of being hard to build.
  • Flat map art: the traditional type of map art, with ordinary image quality and a relatively simple build.

  • File-only map art: the best image quality a vanilla map art can reach. It cannot be built, and usually can only be obtained with commands. If you do not need the map art to exist in the game as blocks, but only to be displayed on a map and to be able to hang in an item frame, choose this option.

    Note that this kind of file-only map art requires at least replacing files in your save, and may also require commands. It is generally only usable in single-player games, or if you are a server administrator.

Here I chose 3D map art.

docs.title: 1.3 Set the block list
docs.text:
The block list is in fact the "material list", or "palette", of a map art. It determines which colors the palette of the map art contains, and which block each color corresponds to.

This page is relatively complex, so I will introduce every part in turn. (In fact, you usually do not need to adjust the block list yourself at all)

The slider area shows every base color. In the Enable box you can check whether SlopeCraft is allowed to use this color. By default every available base color is checked except water (some colors are not available in lower versions).

Below the enable box are the blocks corresponding to each color. In the palette every color can only use one block.

  • You may think that many blocks in the figure have different colors, but note that they are exactly the same in the "eyes of the map"; the only basis for choosing is whether the block is easy to mass-produce.
  • Some base colors only have one usable block, and the palette cannot have holes, so this option cannot be changed — like the glass or emerald block (not shown in the figure) in the figure, it must be selected.

There are four block list presets to choose from at the top:

  • Vanilla is "the original flavor", trying to use the "original block" of each color. It suits creative mode better and is not suitable for survival builds.
  • Cheap tries hard to pick the cheapest blocks, making sure every block can be mass-produced. It suits the early stage of survival.
  • Elegant tries to pick "the most elegant blocks" while still being usable in survival, for example blocks that endermen cannot steal away, that look good and are not too hard to mass-produce. This is the default option.
  • Shiny is made for shaders: it picks glowing blocks as much as possible, striving to be gorgeous enough with shaders.
  • Custom means you are using a custom block list.

A block list preset shows how many colors this map art can use. If you disable some base colors, this number decreases a bit. So the richer the palette and the larger the map art, the better the image quality.

The prefer concrete and other buttons in the upper right corner are there for bulk operations; their meaning is rather obvious and needs no explanation.

docs.title: Saving and loading presets
docs.text:
You can export the current block list so that you can load it next time. The file is stored in json and its suffix is .sc_preset_json.

When you are done with these settings, click the Import images and convert tab at the top to go to the next step.

docs.title: Step 2. Import images and convert
docs.text: On this page you need to finish two small steps: import images, and convert them into map arts.

docs.title: 2.1 Import images
docs.text:
What is the 'project pool'?

SlopeCraft 5.1 introduced a new feature: the "project pool". Every image you import is created as a project by the program, and the subsequent conversion operations add data to the project.

The project pool works like a system file manager: select a single image to preview it or to perform the corresponding operations.

Simply put, you can now do batch operations conveniently! Note: one batch of images can only use one conversion algorithm; images with very different styles or colors should be processed in separate batches!

In the project pool, click Add to import one or more preprocessed images.

If your original image has transparent or semi-transparent pixels, a window to set the transparent pixel handling strategy pops up automatically. The details are as follows:

The transparent pixel handling strategy handles fully transparent pixels (alpha=0) and semi-transparent pixels (alpha>0) in different ways. A fully transparent pixel is either replaced with the background color or set to air; a semi-transparent pixel can be replaced with the background color, blended over the background color, or have its transparency ignored and be treated directly as an opaque pixel. The background color can also be set: the default is the light gray of tiled snow blocks, and you can also choose pure white or any custom color.

Note: transparent pixels are processed when importing. If you are not satisfied with the result, delete the project from the project pool and import the image again.

When the import finishes, the corresponding project appears in the project pool on the left; select a project to preview it.

docs.title: 2.2 Convert images
docs.text: With all the preparation above done, it is time for the main course: converting images into map arts.

docs.title: Choosing a conversion algorithm
docs.text:
The Convert current image button adjusts the colors of the image to colors available in the palette of the map art, while Original and Converted above the preview box show the original image and the adjusted map art respectively, so you can compare them.

There are 5 conversion algorithms above, representing 5 ways of adjusting colors. Dither uses the Floyd-Steinberg algorithm, trying to mix several similar colors to fit the original image better.

The first five conversion algorithms correspond to five different color difference formulas. Among the algorithms, RGB+ is the most recommended, RGB and XYZ are the fastest, and Lab94 and Lab00 give better results but are slower.

For the same image, these 5 kinds of adjustment all give different results.

We all want the map art to be as close to the original as possible, so you can try each kind of adjustment in turn, comparing back and forth with the two buttons, and choose the one that works best.

Before conversion After conversion

Adjusting the image may be slow, especially for large images. If the progress bar suddenly stalls, or even the window stops responding, please do not close the window: do nothing and just wait patiently. Adjusting the image involves a lot of computation; the lag is normal.

docs.title: Convert all images (a special batch operation)
docs.text:
When you have chosen the algorithm you like best, click Convert all to convert every project in the project pool. Converted projects should have a ✔ at their lower right corner.

Once all images are converted (make sure every project has a ✔ at its lower right corner), it is time for the last step of generating map arts: export.

docs.title: Step 3. Export
docs.text:
There are 6 export types. The table below records how the map art types relate to the export types.

Export type 3D map art Flat map art File-only map art Litematica schematic (*.litematic) ✔ ✔ Vanilla structure block file (*.nbt) ✔ ✔ WE schematic (*.schem) ✔ ✔ Map data file (*.dat) ✔ ✔ ✔ Converted image (*.png *.jpg) ✔ ✔ ✔ Flat diagram (*.png *.jpg) ✔

Note: WE schematics (*.schem) are only supported in 1.13+. In 1.12, WE uses the old schematic format with the *.schematic suffix, which SlopeCraft does not support at the moment.

On the export page, choose the type you need and configure it accordingly.

Since the first four export types involve 3D structures, their settings differ considerably from the map data file type, so both are introduced below. (Click a type name to jump there.)

docs.title: 3.a Export as Litematica schematic / vanilla structure block file / WE schematic / flat diagram
Compressing the height (has no effect on flat map arts)
docs.text:
SlopeCraft supports two compression methods: lossy and lossless.

Simply put, lossless compression compresses the total height of the map art under the premise of strictly keeping the color of every pixel unchanged, at the cost of continuity, but its constraints are strong and it may not work out as you wish. It is no exaggeration to say that some images are incompressible, such as a pure white part. That is when a new compression technique is needed: intelligent lossy compression.

Lossy compression then slightly adjusts the colors of individual pixels to compress the total height of the map art so that it is less than or equal to the maximum allowed height specified by the user. Lossy compression is implemented with a genetic algorithm, which belongs to population artificial intelligence and is the most technically advanced module in SlopeCraft at the moment. Do not set the maximum allowed height below 14, otherwise a 3D map art is very likely to fail to compress.

Generally speaking, the smaller the maximum allowed height of lossy compression, the more obvious the loss of image quality. Below, this image would be 255 blocks tall as a 3D map art, and is now lossily compressed (with lossless compression enabled as well). Figure 1 is the build result with a maximum height of 100 blocks, and figure 2 with a maximum height of 20 blocks.

Figure 1 Figure 2

There is no significant change before and after compression and the damage to image quality is not obvious. But on close inspection you can still see some gray dots in the white margins on both sides, and figure 2 has more gray dots than figure 1 because it is compressed more. In addition, a genetic algorithm is a stochastic optimization algorithm, so the modified pixels have a certain randomness and form no obvious regular pattern.

Lossy and lossless compression can be used together or separately. But generally speaking, if lossy compression is enabled, there is no reason not to enable lossless compression. Pure lossy compression needs to modify more pixels, which damages image quality more, while lossless compression can finish the compression with fewer modified pixels, largely reducing the damage.

You can check these two options for flat map arts, but they will not play any role.

docs.title: Bridging
docs.text:
Every horizontal slice of a 3D map art contains many scattered blocks, which are extremely inconvenient to build. If multiple pathways could connect these scattered blocks, building would undoubtedly become much easier. Bridging is the process of connecting all blocks within a horizontal plane with glass blocks to form pathways, which helps the player build.

Undoubtedly bridging consumes extra glass, so it is not recommended to bridge every single layer of a 3D map art. By default a bridge is built every 4 layers, and you can change this interval. Too large an interval weakens the help of the bridges; too small an interval wastes glass.

For more details on map art compression and bridging, read Principles of map arts.

AbrasiveBoar902 provided great help in optimizing the performance of bridging; thanks to him.

docs.title: Other options
docs.text:
• Fire-proof / enderman-proof: as the name suggests, this protects flammable blocks and keeps endermen from stealing things. The method is to wrap every exposed face of these blocks with glass; I tested it and it works. But it also consumes a lot of glass, so choose carefully.

  • Connect mushroom blocks: a map art generated by SlopeCraft may contain several adjacent mushroom blocks (including red mushroom block, brown mushroom block and mushroom stem), whose touching faces should be pore faces but are not in the generated schematic. This feature searches for all adjacent mushroom blocks and fixes their touching faces into pore faces.

docs.title: Extra export options
docs.text:
The first four export types each accept extra export options and attach extra metadata; each is introduced below.

  • Options of Litematica schematics

    In the schematic name and schematic area name fields you can fill in information about the schematic file. It is not mandatory.

  • Options of vanilla structure block files

    Vanilla structure block files are stored as a sparse matrix: wherever nothing is stored there is a structure void. This storage makes structure block files the most vanilla-compatible but worst-compressing format.

    Therefore structure block files have two choices for storing air blocks: as structure void, or stored as-is. Storing air as structure void saves a lot of space, but when pasted out in a structure block it cannot overwrite other non-air blocks; storing it as air blocks overcomes this problem, but the file size becomes very large.

  • Options of WE schematics

    WE schematics have a few more properties. They come from reverse engineering the schematics generated by WorldEdit and correspond directly to nbt tags of the same name. I do not know how these meta properties affect the schematic, because I hardly ever use WE.

  • Exporting flat diagrams

    Sets whether the exported diagram contains split lines, and the interval of the split lines.

docs.title: Pre-building the 3D structure for preview (optional)
docs.text:
Click Pre-build 3D structure and SlopeCraft will build the map art into a 3D structure with the current settings, then show the size and total block count of the schematic.

The pre-built 3D structure is only used for preview, not for exporting.

Note: if the y size of the schematic exceeds 256 / 3841, then by all means do not continue exporting. A schematic that exceeds the height limit is meaningless!

After pre-building the 3D structure, you can do the following two detailed previews:

  • Preview the compression result: lossy compression may further change the image, and here you can check the state of the image.
  • Preview the material list: preview the quantity of materials.
Preview map art Preview material list

docs.title: Export all
docs.text: Once the settings are confirmed, click Export all and choose the folder to export all files into (an empty folder is recommended for batch operations).

docs.title: 3.b Export as map (data) files
docs.text:
Click the Map data file option to jump to the corresponding page.

This page shows the number of rows and columns of the maps corresponding to the map art, the number of files, and the file names of the map data files to be exported.

docs.title: Setting the initial number of the map data files
docs.text:
A map data file is named like map_i.dat, where i is an integer greater than or equal to 0, such as map_3.dat. i is the number of this map data file. The number is in fact the unique identifier of the map data file. Normally the map data files we generate should not overwrite unrelated map data files, so setting the initial number needs extra care.

Pressing F3 + H in the game shows item details, including the id of the map item, that is, the number of the corresponding map data file. The map item shown below corresponds to a map data file named map_6.dat.

There are the following two ways to obtain the maps; pick whichever you like. The way you import them into the game afterwards also differs, so pay attention!

  • If you want to obtain the maps with the /give command:

    The initial number can be anything, as long as it does not overwrite unrelated maps.

  • If you do not want to use commands and only replace the map data files:

    1. First create the n maps corresponding to the map art, where n is the number of map data files shown by SlopeCraft — 4 in this example.

    2. Press F3 + H in the game and check the numbers of the corresponding map data files. These maps should have the numbers a~(a+n-1), n in total.

    3. Exit the world and fill the value of a into the initial number of map data files field in SlopeCraft.

Once the settings are confirmed, click Export and choose the folder to export all files into (an empty folder is recommended).

docs.title: Step 4. Import the map art into the game
docs.text: Jump to: | Import Litematica schematics | Import structure block files | Import WE schematics | Import map data files |

docs.title: Importing Litematica schematics
docs.text:
Open the folder you just exported into and move the exported schematic to the .minecraft2/schematic folder. Then open Minecraft, enter your save/server, and import this schematic where you want to create the map art.

When placing the schematic, note that the x and z coordinates of the schematic origin must be -65+k×128, where k is any integer. The y coordinate can be anything. For example, (63,62,-65). Only then can the map art be aligned with the grid of the map.

Then start building this schematic, or just paste it. When finished, create new maps in the map interior. Each map should be unscaled, because each pixel corresponds to one block. Arrange them in order in item frames, and you are done.

  • If it is a 2×2 map art, you should create 2×2, that is 4, maps.
  • If your game version is 1.14 or later, it is best to lock the maps with glass panes in a cartography table.

docs.title: Importing structure block files
docs.text:
The directory for structure blocks is .minecraft2/saves//generated/minecraft/structures

If you cannot find this directory, the game has not created it yet; you can create it manually and copy the files into it.

When loading the structure later, note that the x and z coordinates of the structure origin must be -65+k×128, where k is any integer. The y coordinate can be anything. For example, (63,62,-65). Only then can the map art be aligned with the grid of the map.

Using structure blocks is rather complicated, so it is not covered here; see this bilibili tutorial.

docs.title: Importing WE schematics
docs.text:
The directory for WorldEdit schematics is .minecraft2/config/worldedit/schematics

If the directory does not exist, the game has not created it yet; you can create it manually and copy the files into it.

Afterwards, in the game you can import the schematic with the //schem load <schematic name> command. See WorldEdit tutorials for details, for example this one.

docs.title: Importing map data files
docs.text:
Open the folder you just exported into and move the exported map data files to the .minecraft2/saves//data folder.

A "replace or skip files" window may pop up. If you are worried about overwriting unrelated maps, you can leave it for now and read on.

  • Obtaining the maps with the /give command:

    This way should not trigger the "replace or skip files" window. If it does, close the window and check whether the map numbers conflict.

    • In 1.12, use /give @s filled_map 1 i to get the map with number i.
    • In 1.13+, use /give @s filled_map{map:i} to get the map with number i.

  • Not using commands, only replacing the map data files:

    1. When you moved the files just now, the "replace or skip files" window should have popped up; click "Replace the files in the destination" to replace the files.

    2. Open the game; these n maps should have been successfully replaced with the map art.

docs.title: 🛠 Advanced features
docs.text: Some advanced operations can be found in the "Advanced" menu. Each is introduced below.

docs.title: Testing the block list
docs.text:
Missing blocks in a schematic are almost always caused by mis-spelled ids. If you import many blocks at once, this feature quickly tests every block in the block list for id errors.

Testing the block list generates a special structure block file containing every available block of every base color (except those that do not match the version). In the structure file every block is arranged in the order of the block list.

If everything is fine, no block will be missing; otherwise the corresponding block has an id error.

The figures below show the effect. Because the schematic is long, it is split into two screenshots.

Left half Right half

docs.title: Outputting the current color table
docs.text:
This menu item lets the user output the current color table as a \(16\times 16\) png image containing all colors currently available.

1.19 3D 1.19 flat 1.19 file-only What is it for?

Outputting the color table is in effect exporting a "palette", which makes pixel art creation easier.

If you want to draw by yourself and use the result in the game, follow the steps below to avoid unexpected errors:

  1. First finish the settings on the "map art configuration" page, so that you can output the color table you want
  2. Export the color table in the advanced menu
  3. Import the color table into your image editing software, draw, and export the image
  4. Do the "map art configuration" settings again (if you closed the software), and import the image
  5. When converting the image, choose the RGB+ algorithm and do not check dither
  6. The remaining export steps are the same as the normal flow; see above

docs.title: 🛠 Custom block lists
docs.text: If you are not satisfied with the presets I provided and want to add other vanilla blocks or even mod blocks yourself, this chapter tells you how to add and use custom blocks in SlopeCraft.

docs.title: Preliminary information
docs.text:
You need to know the following information about a block:

  1. The complete id of the block, including the namespace prefix and all block properties.

    For example, the upper slab of a waxed copper block:

    minecraft:waxed_copper_slab[type=top,waterlogged=false]

    Here minecraft: is the namespace prefix of the vanilla block, and the content in the square brackets is all block properties. To be safe, you should set a corresponding value for every block property.

  2. The earliest game version in which the block appears

    SlopeCraft uses the following values in block lists to refer to major versions:

    Value Version "ANCIENT" Earlier than 1.12 "MC12" 1.12 "MC13" 1.13 "MC14" 1.14 "MC15" 1.15 "MC16" 1.16 "MC17" 1.17 "MC18" 1.18 "MC19" 1.19 "MC20" 1.20 "MC21" 1.21 "MC26_1" 26.1 "MC26_2" 26.2 "MC26_3" 26.3 65535 Future versions

    Normally you should not use 65535, it is only a reserved value. If you insist on assigning a block to a future version, then everything that results is undefined behavior — I do not know what will happen either.

  3. The id of the block in 1.12

    This property was added because Mojang changed quite a few block ids when updating from 1.12 to 1.13. If the block you want to add did not exist in 1.12, or its id did not change, you can fill in an empty string.

  4. The base color of the block

    This is probably the easiest place to make mistakes. For vanilla blocks you can look it up on the Minecraft Wiki. If it is a block added by a mod, either figure out how to measure it yourself, or ask the mod developer.

    If you do not know what a base color is, read Principles of map arts

  5. The Chinese name of the block

  6. The English name of the block
  7. Whether the block needs other blocks attached below it
  8. Whether the block glows
  9. Whether the block is flammable
  10. Whether the block can be stolen by an enderman
  11. The texture image of the block (a 16*16 pixel png image is recommended)

docs.title: Blocks and the block list
docs.text:
In SlopeCraft, block lists are stored in json format, and the related images are placed in the FixedBlocks and CustomBlocks folders.

Block lists come in two kinds: fixed block lists and custom block lists. The fixed block list is the most basic set of blocks I provide, stored in FixedBlocks.json (the corresponding images are in the FixedBlocks folder), making sure every base color has a corresponding block. Although the blocks in the block list are in fact determined only at program runtime, you should not modify it.

Custom block lists are stored in CustomBlocks.json, with the corresponding images in the CustomBlocks folder. This is the user-defined block list, which allows the user to edit it flexibly. I wrote some slab blocks in there as a reference.

Each block has the following properties:

Property name Type Required Default Description baseColor byte yes The base color of the block on the map id string yes Block id, including the namespace and detailed block states version byte yes The earliest version in which the block appears. nameZH string yes The Chinese name of the block nameEN string yes The English name of the block icon string yes The file name of the image of the block idOld string no empty string The id of the block in 1.12 needGlass bool no false Whether the bottom of the block must have other blocks isGlowing bool no false Whether the block is glowing endermanPickable bool no false Whether the block can be stolen by an enderman burnable bool no false Whether the block can be burned

The property wallUseable has been removed, because wall map arts have been removed.

In json format it looks like this:

{
    "baseColor": 11,
    "id": "minecraft:cobblestone_slab[type=top,waterlogged=false]",
    "nameZH": "圆石台阶",
    "nameEN": "Cobblestone slab",
    "icon": "cobblestone_slab.png",
    "version": "ANCIENT",
    "idOld": "minecraft:stone_slab[half=top,variant=cobblestone]"
}

The json above shows the information of a cobblestone top slab, parsed as follows:

  1. Its base color is 11, which is also the base color of cobblestone, stone bricks and stone.
  2. Its block id is "minecraft:cobblestone_slab[type=top,waterlogged=false]"; the block state in the square brackets says that it is a top slab and does not contain water;
  3. Its Chinese name is "圆石台阶" and its English name is "Cobblestone slab";
  4. Its image is a file named "cobblestone_slab.png", placed in the CustomBlocks folder;
  5. Its earliest version is 0, which means it was added before 1.12;
  6. Because its block id changed in 1.13, its block id in 1.12 is the value of idOld.

You have found the end of the world (=・ω・=). Here is a cluster amaryllis as a reward.

  1. The build height differs between versions and dimensions. See the Wiki for details. ↩

  2. Save data and configs are not necessarily stored directly in the .minecraft folder; the actual paths depend on version isolation. Take the saves folder as an example: if version isolation is off, the saves directory is .minecraft/saves, otherwise it is .minecraft/versions/<your game version>/saves. ↩↩↩↩

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
VisualCraft is a brand-new Minecraft pixel art generator developed by the MC player TokiNoBug, and it is a subproject of SlopeCraft. Unlike other similar software, VisualCraft aims to keep up with the latest MC versions (1.12 ~ the latest), support as many MC features as possible, and provide the most powerful functions.

At the moment VisualCraft can parse many third-party resource packs, and also allows adding custom blocks. Different from the traditional approach, VisualCraft parses resource packs in terms of block models, staying as close to what Minecraft does as possible, so all kinds of custom block models are supported.

As for export, VisualCraft supports Litematica mod schematics (*.litematic), WorldEdit schematics (*.shem)(1.13+ only), vanilla structure block files (*.nbt), flat diagrams (*.png) and so on.

VisualCraft supports stacking various transparent blocks on top of each other to produce more colors. The software supports at most 65534 colors; limited by this, the number of layers of a pixel art does not exceed 3.

Because the number of colors is so large, VisualCraft uses GPU acceleration. The supported API is currently Vulkan, but it can also compute on CPU only.

docs.title: Step 0. GPU settings
docs.text:
This step is not compulsory. You can skip it, but if your image is very large, or you want to generate a pixel art of 3 layers, this step greatly improves the efficiency of VisualCraft.

Up to now there are two compute options: the number of CPU threads and the compute device.

In the first box you can set the number of CPU threads. The default value is the logical thread count of your CPU, coming from the return value of std::thread::hardware_concurrency(). You can set it a bit larger so that the CPU cores are used better, but too many threads add extra burden to the thread scheduler, which costs more time and consumes more power.

In the next radio box you can choose a compute device. This device is only used during image conversion, and all available devices are listed in the small tree widget on the right. Only Vulkan is supported as an API for now. For macOS, which has no official Vulkan support, I am trying various community solutions.

If VisualCraft was built without a GPU API, then only CPU computation is available and GPU acceleration cannot be used.

docs.title: Step 1. Basic attributes
docs.text:
On the first page you can set the basic attributes. On the left you can set the pixel art direction and the Minecraft version, while biome, max layers and transparent leaves can be set below.

The pixel art direction and the MC version are self-evident, while the last three options need to be explained.

  1. Max layers refers to the maximum number of block layers of the pixel art, because VisualCraft supports stacking transparent blocks on non-transparent blocks.
    • Max layers should be a positive number and no greater than 3, otherwise the number of colors will exceed 65535, which is beyond the range of uint16_t.
  2. Biome refers to the biome of the place where the pixel art is built.
    • In Minecraft, the colors of grass, leaves and vines depend on the biome, so it is necessary to input the biome.
  3. Transparent leaves refers to whether leaves are treated as transparent blocks.
    • The appearance of leaves depends on the render options. If the graphics quality is not low, leaves are transparent blocks; otherwise they are opaque, and the transparent pixels in their texture are replaced with black (0x000000).

Resource packs and block state lists (BSL) can be set on the right. A resource pack is a zip that can be given to Minecraft, and a BSL is a json file that stores block information. Only blocks recorded in a BSL can be used by VisualCraft.

Resource packs and BSLs are shown in two lists. Click Add and you can select a file and add it to the list. To remove one or more items from the list, select them and click Remove. Note that only the selected items can be removed. You can sort the items by dragging them. If you want to use an item, check its checkbox, otherwise leave it unchecked. When several resource packs are parsed, they stack in the order of the list, just as Minecraft does. Several BSLs stack in the same way as resource packs.

Vanilla resource pack and vanilla json are special items that cannot be removed, because they represent the base resource pack and the base BSL respectively. But you can still disable them by unchecking their checkboxes.

If you have finished setting the basic attributes, click Load resources in the Resource menu and VisualCraft will load these resources.

docs.title: Step 2. Set the allowed blocks
docs.text: After loading resources, all available blocks appear on the second page, separated by category. You can select or deselect any single block and any category.

docs.title: Hot keys
docs.text:
The hot keys on the left make selecting or disabling blocks more convenient. To eliminate ambiguity, note that: in the following text, "select" and "enable" mean the same thing, and "disable" and "uncheck" also mean the same thing.

Key name Effect Select all Select all blocks Deselect all Deselect all blocks Disable non-reproducible Disable all non-reproducible blocks Disable rare blocks Disable all rare blocks Select reversely classwise Reverse the selection of each category, without affecting the checkboxes of blocks Select reversely blockwise Reverse the selection of all blocks, without affecting the checkboxes of categories Advanced matching Pops up a subwindow that lets you match blocks by custom rules and set them as selected or unselected

After finishing the settings above, find the Resource menu and click Set allowed blocks to set the allowed blocks.

docs.title: Step 3. Load images
docs.text:
In fact, from a minimalist point of view, all you need to do is add images and then go to the next page. In this section I will introduce the widgets of this page.

After you set the allowed blocks, the number of colors is shown after conversion algorithm.

There are several algorithms that can convert images into pixel arts. VisualCraft and SlopeCraft use almost the same set of algorithms, so these options are the same. The only difference is that VisualCraft can be GPU accelerated, because it may have to handle more than 10 thousand colors and much larger images.

The logic of importing images is similar to that of importing resource packs and BSLs. Click + to add images and - to remove the selected images. VisualCraft was designed as a batch processing tool from the beginning, so all images are placed in one list. If you click an image, it is displayed and converted.

You can change the display options. Turn on Display original size to force all images to be displayed at their original size regardless of the label size. Select Display original and Display converted to decide whether to show the corresponding images.

docs.title: Step 4. Export
docs.text:
On this page you can tell VisualCraft how to export pixel arts and images. 5 export types are supported.

Type File name extension Description Litematica *.litematic Litematica mod schematic Structure block file *.nbt Vanilla structure block file WE schematic *.schem WorldEdit mod schematic (1.13+) Converted image *.png *.jpg The converted image Flat diagram *.png A flat diagram formed by replacing every pixel with the corresponding block

Since VisualCraft is inherently a batch processing tool, you can select a type in the radio box and then click Set export destination to set the folder for the generated files. This operation fills the exported file names into the related columns.

If you want to change the way of exporting, just edit the export table. The third to the seventh columns are editable.

When you click Start, VisualCraft executes according to the table. If a cell is empty, it is skipped; otherwise the file name in that cell is parsed. If the extension is incorrect, an error may occur.

It is worth noting that a flat diagram may consist of several images, because a pixel art may have several layers. So the text in the cell is in fact a list of file names separated by semicolons ";" (note: half-width characters!). For example:

# Two layers
D:/image00_layer0.png;D:/image00_layer1.png
# Three layers
D:/image01_layer0.png;D:/image01_layer1.png;D:/image01_layer2.png
# One layer
D:/image01_layer0.png

If the number of semicolons is incorrect, an error will occur as well.

docs.title: Export options
docs.text:
On this page you can set the attributes of the exported files. The options of Litematica schematics, structure block files and WE schematics are the same as those in SlopeCraft, while the flat diagram options are worth explaining.

Since the flat diagram represents the whole pixel art with blocks, it is useful to draw horizontal and vertical lines to split the whole image into chunks. By default a split line is drawn every 16 blocks, which is the size of a Minecraft chunk. You can change the margin in the spin box, or check the checkbox to disable the split lines.

The flat diagram is generated by libpng, and it really is a large image, so you can tell libpng how to compress the image through png compression level. The ranges of the two level numbers are [0,9]. A larger compression level means better compression and more encoding time, while a larger memory level means more memory is used. If you are not familiar with image and file compression, just keep the default values.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
Warning

Before submitting an issue, please make sure that the bug has been fixed in the latest version!

  1. Can I use it on Bedrock Edition/Netease version?

    • I have never played these versions, so I don't know if it can be used, and I don't know how to use it.
    • Theoretically, as long as the version is Java and Litematica mod is installed successfully, it can be used.
    • There is no Litematica mod for Bedrock Edition, so, in theory, it can't be used.

  2. I want to build in a server, but the server doesn't have the Litematica mod installed.

    • First of all, in the interface and all documents of this software, we only needs the Litematica mod developed by Masa. Any other mods with the word "projection" or similar functions are not what we need.
    • Litematica mod is a client mod, server installation is not needed. Only the client needs to install Litematica and its dependency mod Malilib, and then the projection mod can be used normally. So don't ask this kind of stupid question anymore.
    • Litematica Mod - CurseForge
    • Litematica Mod - MC Mod

  3. Where is SlopeCraft.exe/SlopeCraft.app/SlopeCraft Executable File?

    • DO! NOT! DOWNLOAD THE SOURCE CODE!!!
    • How to download the application from GitHub: On the repo page, there is a release section on the right side of the page. Click it and you can see the download links.

  4. How to make a non-square pixel arts?

    • Why do people think that SlopeCraft can't make non-square pixel arts?
    • SlopeCraft will never scale your image, but reproduce each pixel as it is. You can make any size of pixel arts, just handle it normally.

  5. Why is the picture almost gray after adjusting the color in SlopeCraft? / Why is the color not ideal / ...

    • There is some color that are set by Mojang, and there are some colors that don't have a similar map color, such as light blue, gray blue, light pink, light purple, etc. You can only find colors that don't differ too much.
    • A dithering algorithm has been implemented in v3.5, which can solve this problem.

  6. Why can't I get the map item with the /give command?

    • In 1.12, use /give @p filled_map 1 i to get the map with the serial number i
    • In 1.13+, use /give @p filled_map{map:i} to get the map with the serial number i

  7. Can I scale down the map?

    • It is not recommended to scale down the map, because the resolution of the map is still 128*128 pixels, no matter whether it is scaled down or not, and the quality will only be reduced. The best way to increase the resolution is to use multiple maps without scaling.

docs.title: Principal of Map Pixel Art
docs.text:
This article will introduce the working principle of map pixel art in form of 3D map, 2D map and map data file. SlopeCraft was developed based on these mechanisms. By studying and using these mechanisms, people can make the map display custom images.

Tip

Map mentionned in this article refers to the map item in Minecraft rather than the saving file.

docs.title: Why are we using maps?
docs.text:
We can seperate Minecraft pixel art into two types: visual and map. Visual map pixel art is built to be viewed directly. It can be placed horizontally (on the floor or on the ceiling) or vertically (on the wall). It is straightforward and simple, but it is often very large and not very convenient to view. However, maps can be placed in item frames and displayed on the floor or walls. Multiple maps can even be placed together to form a large image. This is the advantage of maps.

In visual pixel art, blocks shows the color of their texture directly. Each block is different. However, this is not the case for map pixel art. The color shown on the map might be slightly different from the color of the texture, and many blocks have the same color, such as snow and white concrete. In addition, for most blocks, the color shown on the map have some minor but noticeable differences from the color on the placed block. Many visual pixel art looks bad on the map because of this. So the first thing to do is to understand the mechanism of Minecraft maps.

docs.title: How does the map show blocks?
docs.text:
The resolution of each map is 128 × 128 pixels, regardless of the scale. The area shown by the map is determined by the scale, which is an integer ranging from 0 to 4 (including 0 and 4). The area shown by the map is a square, with a length and width of \(128\times 2^{Scale}\). When scale is 0, the map corresponds to a 128 × 128 range of blocks, where each pixel represents a block; otherwise, each pixel represents \(2^{Scale}\) blocks. Maps with scale greater than 0 are meaningless for map pixel art, so I won't discuss them anymore, but I will tell you why they are meaningless.

To make the map easier to put together, each map will automatically align with a grid. The starting coordinate of the map (the northwest corner) is \((128\times 2^{Scale}-64,y,128\times 2^{Scale}-64)\).

The table below shows the relationship between the coordinate axis and the four directions.

Direction Map Direction Coordinate Axis Direction North Up z- South Down z+ West Left x- East Right x+

  1. How does Minecraft store map data?

    In Minecraft Java Edition, the content of the map is not stored in each map item, but in the data folder. Their file names are in the form of map_i.dat, where i is a natural number under 2,147,483,647 (32767 in 1.12). i is the map number, and each map item in the game only stores the corresponding map number.

    For example, if a player holds a map with number 114, when the save is loaded, Minecraft will find the map data file named map_114.dat and load it. Then its content will be displayed on the map. Therefore, the essence of the map is not the item, but the map data file.

    Nearly all the data of the map is stored in the map data file, including but not limited to each pixel. The most important thing about the map is how the map data is stored.

  2. Map pixels and MapColor

    Each pixel of the map is an 8-bit unsigned integer, ranging from 0 to 255. Since the map data file is in compressed NBT format, the map pixels are stored in a byte array containing 16384 elements (although the byte in NBT format is a signed integer, it doesn't matter to treat it as an unsigned integer). This 128 × 128 pixel matrix is stored in row prioritized order.

    This determines that each pixel may have at most 256 colors, and each value corresponds to a different color. This 8-bit unsigned integer is the map color. We can say that the map is an 8-bit index image with a fixed color table.

  3. BaseColor and Shadow

    As mentioned above, the map color is an 8-bit unsigned integer. The high 6 bits form an 6-bit unsigned integer, which is the base color (BaseColor), and the remaining 2 bits form another 2-bit unsigned integer, which is the the shadow. The relationship between the map color, the base color and the shadow is:

    \[ MapColor = 4 \times BaseColor + Shadow \]

    The base color depends on the block type. There may be up to 64 base colors in the game. As of the latest version (1.17 when this article was written), 62 base colors have been used in the game; in 1.16, 59 base colors were used, and each base color had a corresponding color (RGB); from 1.12 to 1.15, 52 base colors were used. Unused base colors have no corresponding color, and they are meaningless to the map.

    On Minecraft wiki, there is a table of base colors and blocks: Map Item Format.

    But the base color is not the color of the map color. The R, G, and B components of the base color must be multiplied by a factor, and then divided by 255 (rounded down) to get the color of the map color. This factor is determined by the shadow value.

    Shadow Factor 0 180 1 220 2 255 3 135

    As you can see, the map color with shadow value 2 is the same as the base color, the map color with shadow value 1 is slightly darker, the map color with shadow value 0 is darker, and the map color with shadow value 3 is the darkest.

    What is the meaning of the shadow? The shadow represents the relative height of a block compared to the surrounding blocks. If the coordinates of block A are \((x,y_A,z)\), and the coordinates of the block B northbound of A are \((x,y_B,z-1)\), then the shadow value of A is

    \[ Shadow(A)=\left\{ \begin{aligned} 0\quad,&\quad \text{if } y_A<y_B \\ 1\quad,&\quad \text{if } y_A=y_B \\ 2\quad,&\quad \text{if } y_A>y_B \end{aligned} \right. \]

    In all the base colors, water (12) is the most special. The shadow value of water is not related to the relative height, but the water depth. When the water depth is 1, the shadow value is 2; when the water depth is 6, the shadow value is 1; when the water depth is equal to or greater than 11, the shadow value is 0.

    If a block is higher than the block to the north, it will be brighter; (if the water is shallower, it will be brighter), which allows the map to show the ups and downs of the terrain.

    To be noted, the shadow is a 2-bit unsigned integer, which can have 4 values, but only the first 3 are used. The remaining shadow value 3 can work normally on the map, but it is impossible to get in the original survival. I can't figure out what Mojang was thinking.

  4. 0 is a special base color

    Base color 0 represents air or unexplored, which is completely different from all other base colors. The color corresponding to base color 0 is fully transparent, and only the background color of the map item (or the texture of the item frame) can be seen. Many transparent blocks belong to base color 0, such as glass, nether portal, torch, etc. It is very strange that redstone lamp also have a base color 0.

  5. Why is it meaningless to scale the map?

    According to the map mechanism, scaling the map cannot increase the resolution of the map, nor can it bring more colors. So building a larger map by scaling the picture is purely a waste of blocks and space.

docs.title: How does the map pixel art work?
docs.text:
1. 3D map mechanism

    In 3D map pixel arts, blocks are placed in a specific position to form a 3D structure. Each block has two functions:

    • Show the base color of itself
    • Determine the shadow of the block southbound of itself

    As you can see, the height of each block is not random, but determined by the map color.

  2. 2D map mechanism

    If you want the map to be only composed of base colors with shadow value 1 (or water with shadow value 2), you will get a 2D map pixel art. Each block has the same height.

  3. Map data file mechanism

    For both 2D and 3D map pixel arts, you will have to build the generated structure in the game first, and then use the map to record it. This is indeed the only way to build a map pixel art in the vanilla survival mode. But if you don;t care if it is vanilla, you can also replace the map data file directly. The map pixel art in form of data files can be put directly into the saving folder, or replace the existing map data file with the generated one, and then get the corresponding map item with the command. This is the only way to use the third shadow.

docs.title: What is height compression?
docs.text:
Height compression is a new technology that can reduce the maximum height of 3D map pixel arts. Since large map pixel arts can very easily exceed the height limit, compression is very meaningful. Currently, there are two ways of compression: lossless compression and lossy compression.

  1. Lossless compression

    When lossless compression is used, the display effect of the map is completely unchanged. It tries to sink some parts of the map.

    During the compression, SlopeCraft processes each column of the map independently.

    \[ \displaylines{ \Delta H_i=\left\{ egin{aligned} Shadow_i-1\quad &,\quad ext{if }BaseColor_i eq 0,12 \ 0 \quad &,\quad ext{else} \end{aligned} ight. ewline H_i=\sum_{j=0}^i \Delta H_j ewline maxHeight=\max H } \]

    In the formula above, \(\Delta H\) is the height difference between each block and the block northbound, and \(H\) is the height of each block. This formula is slightly different from the actual source code, but the basic principle is the same.

    The formula above limits the height difference to -1, 0 or 1, but this restriction is not necessary. For example, a block with shadow 2 only requires its height difference with the block northbound to be greater than 0, but not necessarily 1. This provides an opportunity for lossless compression.

    Lossless compression also does special processing for water and air blocks, because their shadow values are not related to the height difference. Although this makes the code implementation much more difficult, the compression effect will be better.

    The lossless compression cannot promise to compress the height to 256 or less. Sometimes a column of the map may even be monotonic increasing/decreasing, which is not compressible.

  2. Lossy compression

    Apparently, lossless compression cannot solve the problem completely. To compress the total height of the map to any value, it is also acceptable to slightly adjust the map color of some pixels. The lossy compression algorithm will slightly adjust the map color of some pixels to compress the total height, and also ensure that the color difference is as small as possible.

    Lossy compression can compress the map to any height. Because it is implemented with genetic algorithm, the performance of lossy compression is somewhat random and relatively slow.

    Although the total height can be theoretically compressed to any value, I don't recommend that you set the maximum allowed height to a value less than 14, otherwise the genetic algorithm needs a very looooong time to compress - it may even fail to compress.

    And it is worth mentioning that the above two methods are parallel, you can use both methods at the same time, or only use one. If you have enabled lossy compression, I recommend that you use the lossless compression at the same time, which can reduce the damage to the quality caused by lossy compression.

docs.title: Glass Bridge in 3D Map Pixel Art
docs.text:
If you take any horizontal slice of a 3D map pixel art, you will find that there are many isolated blocks on the slice. This structure is really difficult to build in vanilla survival, even with the help of schematica mod. But if we connect these isolated blocks together, it will be easier to build.

The glass bridge is this "connection". Using Prim algorithm can connect all blocks in a layer with the fewest glass, and this process is called bridge building. Usually, not every layer needs to be bridged, otherwise a lot of glass will be wasted. By default, the interval is 4 layers, which means a bridge will be built every 5 layers.

Considering the time complexity of Prim algorithm is \(O(n^3)\), it will take some time. But compared to the time spent on building, it is actually saving time.

docs.title: Compilation Guide
docs.text:
Welcome to the compilation guide of SlopeCraft. This guide will help you build SlopeCraft. Please read this general guide first, and then read the guide for your platform to complete the build.

Questions

If you meet any problem when building SlopeCraft, please draw us an issue on our GitHub repository.

docs.title: Compilers
docs.text: Currently clang 20+ can be used to build SlopeCraft; in theory any environment that supports C++23 can build it. Windows and Linux are currently built with LLVM Clang, while macOS is built with Apple Clang.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
1. Qt v6.5.0 or later for the GUI
    • If your Qt is built and configured by yourself, make sure you have installed QtBase, QtNetwork and QtTools
    • Qt 6.12 LTS is recommended
  2. Eigen v3.4.0 or later for linear algebra
    • Can be downloaded automatically.
  3. mc_schem for the schematic library
    • Can be downloaded automatically
    • Requires the rust toolchain
  4. gapp for the genetic algorithm
    • Can be downloaded automatically
  5. xsimd for vectorization
    • Can be downloaded automatically
  6. libnbt++ for the NBT library
    • Can be downloaded automatically
  7. Nlohmann json cli11 magic_enum
    • Can be downloaded automatically
  8. libpng libzip zlib boost
    • You must install it, and add the installation path to CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH
  9. 7z for creating archives
    • You must install it, but CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH is not needed

docs.title: Compilation Guide on Windows and Linux
docs.text: This document tells you how to build SlopeCraft on Windows and Linux. Clang (LLVM 20 or later) is strongly recommended; SlopeCraft does not guarantee that MSVC, GCC or a Clang < 20 can build it successfully (although logically they should).

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Install the dependencies manually, or build them yourself.

Or use vcpkg:

vcpkg install --triplet=x64-windows boost-uuid boost-multi-array zlib libpng bzip2  liblzma libzip eigen3 xsimd magic-enum gapp 
# Install the rust toolchain (a separately distributed rust toolchain also works)
rustup toolchain install stable
# If you want GPU acceleration for VisualCraft, the Vulkan components are required
vcpkg install --triplet=x64-windows glslang[tools] vulkan-headers vulkan-memory-allocator vulkan-loader
Besides that, building on Windows also requires Qt. You can use the official Qt installer, or build and install Qt yourself (with MSVC). Qt 6.5 is the minimum; 6.12 LTS is recommended.

docs.title: Linux (Ubuntu)
docs.text:
# Install the build tools and the dependencies such as Eigen, libzip and boost
sudo apt install cmake ninja-build clang-20 libomp-20-dev xz-utils bzip2 libzip-dev zipcmp ziptool zipmerge libpng-dev libeigen3-dev libexpected-dev p7zip-full libboost-all-dev libboost-tools-dev libboost-doc
# Install the rust toolchain (a rust toolchain installed by the package manager also works)
rustup toolchain install stable
# Install Qt6 on Ubuntu. Other Linux distributions are similar
sudo apt install libqt6widgets6 libqt6gui6 libqt6network6 qt6-base-dev qt6-tools-dev-tools qt6-tools-dev qt6-l10n-tools x11-utils libxcb-xinerama0 libxv1 libgl-dev
# Dependencies of the Vulkan SDK
sudo apt-get install libglm-dev libxcb-dri3-0 libxcb-present0 libpciaccess0 libxcb-keysyms1-dev libxcb-dri3-dev libx11-dev libwayland-dev libxrandr-dev libxcb-randr0-dev libxcb-ewmh-dev python-is-python3 bison libx11-xcb-dev liblz4-dev libzstd-dev ocaml-core pkg-config libxml2-dev wayland-protocols python3-jsonschema clang-format qtbase5-dev

docs.title: Build SlopeCraft
docs.text:
1. Clone the SlopeCraft repository and enter the repository directory

    git clone https://github.com/SlopeCraft/SlopeCraft.git

  2. Configure CMake

    Run CMake to configure this project. Command line examples:

    • Windows

      .../vcvars64.bat
cmake -S . -B ./build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-cl -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang-cl -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=install -DSlopeCraft_GPU_API=Vulkan -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=...
      • When compiling with clang-cl, you should first call vcvars64.bat to set the environment variables required by MSVC (clang-cl mimics the MSVC compiler). This file can be found in the Visual Studio installation directory. Its default location is probably C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\Community\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvars64.bat
      • You should put the installation directories of Qt, vcpkg, vulkan and rust into CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH.
      • If the installation directory of vulkan or rust has already been added to the PATH environment variable, it does not need to be added to CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH. If there are multiple paths, separate them with a semicolon ;.

    • Linux

      cmake -S . -B ./build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-20 -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++-20 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=install  -DSlopeCraft_GPU_API=Vulkan -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=...
      - If Vulkan is enabled, you should put the installation directory of vulkan into CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH. - If the default Clang of your system is newer than 20, there is no need to specify the Clang version. - The Vulkan SDK downloaded from apt on Ubuntu 24 is older than 1.3, SlopeCraft cannot use it and will run into a lot of compilation errors.

  3. Build all targets

    cmake --build ./build --parallel

  4. Install

    Run cmake --install to install all binaries and block files. By default the install directory is ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/install, where you can find all executables.

  5. Package

    Run cpack -G <package type> to install again and create a package. The supported package types are currently 7Z, ZIP, TXZ and DEB.

docs.title: Notice
docs.text:
1. If you meet any problem, draw us a new issue.
  2. If you are building VisualCraftL on linux, some linking problems around libzip may occur. To fix this problem, there are 2 ways possible:
    1. Use a static archive of libzip instead of shared lib. But this libzip.a should be compiled with argument -fPIC, because libVisualCraftL.so, a shared lib will link to it.
      • If your libzip.a links other compress libs(for example, lzma), linking may fail. That is because libzip links to its dependents privately regardless of whether libzip is built to be a shared lib. I guess that this is a designing mistake in libzip. So it is deprecated to use a static libzip.
    2. Use shared libzip, and copy libzip.so and symlinks against it to CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR. This is what I'm doing now.

docs.title: Compilation Guide on macOS
docs.text:
This document tells you how to build SlopeCraft on macOS.

Tip

This document tries to make sure that most users can follow it, so it may contain some basic content (for example, how to install Clang). If you already know the part you are reading, feel free to skip it. Since the lead developer ToKiNoBug does not have a macOS device, this document is mainly written based on CI of SlopeCraft, so it's not the only way. If you are familiar with development on macOS, you are welcome to build SlopeCraft however you like.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This document involves command line operations. We recommend using iTerm 2 as your terminal emulator and getting familiar with basic command line usage before you start.

docs.title: Install dependencies
docs.text:
First, make sure that Homebrew is installed (we will use Homebrew to install the dependencies). If you have not installed Homebrew yet, run the following command in the terminal:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

Then we need to install the dependencies that SlopeCraft's build scripts will not install automatically:

  1. Apple clang

    The default C/C++ compiler on macOS is Apple clang, which ships together with the Xcode Command Line Tools and has no separate installer, so installing the command line tools is enough. If it is not installed yet, run the following command in the terminal:

    xcode-select --install

    A window will then pop up: click "Install" and wait for the download and installation to finish. If you already have the full Xcode installed, the command line tools are installed together with Xcode and you can skip this step; if the system reports xcode-select: error: command line tools are already installed, that means it is already installed too.

    It is recommended to check the compiler version with the following command. The version should preferably be at least 21, otherwise it is hard to guarantee good C++23 support. Theoritically you can also use the LLVM clang from Homebrew, but it may run into OpenMP problems as well. 

    /usr/bin/clang++ --version

    If everything is fine, you should see output similar to the following (the exact version numbers change with your Xcode / command line tools version): 

    Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)
Target: x86_64-apple-darwin25.6.0
Thread model: posix
InstalledDir: /Applications/Xcode_26.6.app/Contents/Developer/Toolchains/XcodeDefault.xctoolchain/usr/bin
    Note that Apple clang does not ship an OpenMP runtime, so libomp must be installed in step 4.

  2. Ninja and CMake

    SlopeCraft is built with CMake, and Ninja is the recommended CMake generator, so we need to install CMake and Ninja:

    brew install cmake ninja

    Use ninja --version to check whether Ninja has been installed successfully. If everything is fine, you should see output similar to the following:

    1.11.1

  3. Rust toolchain

    SlopeCraft uses mc_schem, a schematic library written in Rust, so a Rust toolchain is required. We recommend installing and managing Rust with rustup; run the following command in the terminal:

    curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

    This script downloads rustup and lists several installation options; just press Enter to choose the default 1) Proceed with standard installation. When it is done, rustup installs cargo, rustc, rustup and the other commands into ~/.cargo/bin and adds that directory to the shell's PATH, so you need to open a new terminal (or run source "$HOME/.cargo/env") before you can use these commands.

    Then run the following commands to confirm that the toolchain is installed and that stable is the default toolchain:

    rustup default stable
rustc --version
cargo --version

    If everything is fine, both rustc and cargo will print their versions. If you prefer to manage Rust with Homebrew, you can also run brew install rustup and then rustup-init; the result is the same.

  4. Third-party dependencies

    brew install libzip libpng xz bzip2 boost magic_enum xsimd eigen sevenzip libomp

  5. Qt

    Install the shared version of Qt 6: 

    brew install qt

    You can also use a statically linked Qt, but that usually means building Qt yourself. Building Qt is a rather involved process; here is a sample script: 

    git clone https://github.com/qt/qtbase.git --recursive
cd qtbase 
git checkout v6.12.0
cd ..

git clone https://github.com/qt/qttools.git --recursive
cd qttools
git checkout v6.12.0
cd ..

mkdir build install
cd build

# Configure, build and install qtbase
../qtbase/configure --prefix=../install -static -release -nomake tests -skip qtdoc
cmake --build . --parallel
cmake --install .
rm -rf ./*

# Configure, build and install qttools
../install/bin/qt-configure-module ../qttools
cmake --build . --parallel
cmake --install .
rm -rf ./*
    The script above can be run in any directory (as long as there are no permission problems); the static Qt 6.12.0 libraries will be installed into the install subdirectory of the current directory.

docs.title: Build SlopeCraft
docs.text:
1. Clone the SlopeCraft repository and enter the repository directory

    git clone https://github.com/SlopeCraft/SlopeCraft.git && cd SlopeCraft

  2. Configure CMake

    Configure CMake with the following command:

    LIBOMP_PREFIX="$(brew --prefix libomp)"
cmake -S . -B ./build -G Ninja \
    -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=/usr/bin/clang \
    -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=/usr/bin/clang++ \
    -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=./build/install \
    -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
    -DCMAKE_OSX_SYSROOT="$(xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-path)" \
    -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=15.0 \
    -DSlopeCraft_GPU_API:STRING=None \
    -DMC_SCHEM_HAS_mdspan=OFF \
    -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$LIBOMP_PREFIX;/usr/local"

    In the command above we specify several parameters:

    • CMAKE_C_COMPILER specifies the C compiler; it should be /usr/bin/clang, because Apple clang is currently the primary target
    • CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER specifies the path of the C++ compiler; it should be /usr/bin/clang++. In theory both compilers can be switched to LLVM Clang, but they must always match — never mix compilers from different sources
    • CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX specifies the installation path; this guide sets it to ./build/install, you can change it to whatever suits you
    • CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE specifies the build type, such as Debug or Release
    • CMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET specifies the minimum macOS version. It is recommended to set:
    • 13.3 for Apple Silicon devices
    • 15.0 for Intel devices
    • CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH tells CMake where to find packages. It can contain multiple paths separated by ;.

    If you want to use a statically built Qt, you must add the Qt installation directory to CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH; otherwise CMake will not find Qt, or will find another Qt.

    In addition, you can use SlopeCraft_vectorize to enable or disable vectorization. If it is ON, AVX and AVX2 are used on Intel chips and Neon is used on Apple Silicon chips. Vectorization is enabled by default.

    Although SlopeCraft_GPU_API lets you choose the GPU acceleration API, SlopeCraft currently only supports Vulkan for GPU acceleration, and Vulkan has no official support on macOS (yes, Apple really is that self-absorbed — if it can be incompatible, it will be). Community Vulkan implementations have not been tested yet.

  3. Change into the build directory and build SlopeCraft

    Use the following commands to change into build and build SlopeCraft:

    cd build
cmake --build . --parallel

  4. Install

    Use the following command to install SlopeCraft:

    cmake --install .

docs.title: Clean up existing build files
docs.text:
If you want to rebuild from scratch, you can delete the existing build files with the following command:

rm -rf 3rdParty binaries build
